englang_edx.2.0.summary: This point is the genre menu for Paper 2 Section A: both unseen texts are 20th- and 21st-century non-fiction drawn from journalism, speeches, journals, reference book extracts and literary non-fiction. Knowing the expected form tells you why a headline, salutation, glossary, dated entry or reflective voice is there, so evidence can be read as convention rather than decoration. The same real event can be an article, a speech, a letter or travel writing, and the marks come from naming the form precisely and proving it with cues.

core.h: Read the form before the lines
core.p: In Paper 2 Section A the two texts are unseen 20th- and 21st-century non-fiction, so the first move is to name the likely **text type** from title, layout, address, date, headings and register. The form is a contract: it tells you what the writer is allowed to do and what the reader expects next.
bullets: **Text type** is not decoration; it sets purpose, audience, mode and likely conventions.
The same fact can be used differently in an article, a speech, a reference extract or a letter.
Do not decide by topic alone: a travel piece may contain facts, and a reference extract may still select and emphasise.
Unseen means all evidence must come from the extract, not from outside knowledge.
20th- and 21st-century language can date; quote the words rather than assuming modern attitudes.
A mixed form is still answerable: name the dominant form and note the borrowed convention.

callouts.p: A recognised form such as article, review, speech, journal, reference book extract, autobiography, letter or travel writing; its conventions create reader expectations.
You are not asked to know the source; you are asked to identify cues and interpret what they do.
Write the form, audience and mode in the margin before you quote.
A text about football may be a review, a speech, a journal entry or travel writing.

core.p: **Journalism** is public and timely non-fiction for readers. Articles usually inform, explain, describe or argue; **reviews** judge a book, film, performance, product or place against criteria and guide the reader towards a decision.
bullets: Articles often use headline, standfirst, byline, short paragraphs, quotations and captions.
Fact and opinion can sit side by side; the skill is to say which is doing the work.
A review needs criteria, judgement, evidence and often a recommendation or rating.
Register varies by publication: broadsheet seriousness, magazine chat, online urgency.
Presentational features help the reader scan, but the meaning still comes from language choices.
A review is not merely negative; praise can be the judgement.

callouts.p: A text that judges a book, film, performance, product or place against stated or implied criteria and guides the reader.
In a review, ask: what standard is being used, and is the evidence strong enough?
Saying I liked it is not a review convention unless a judgement is supported.

core.p: A **speech** is planned for delivery to an audience on an occasion, even when we read it on the page. Its conventions are oral: address, rhythm, repetition, pause and a build towards a response.
bullets: Look for salutation, occasion and a clear addressee such as ladies and gentlemen or students.
Rhetorical questions, repetition and the rule of three create rhythm and memory.
Contrast and anaphora can make a simple point feel inevitable.
Anecdote personalises; lists can persuade by weight or by climax.
Short sentences and punctuation may signal pause, emphasis or command.
Structure often moves from greeting to issue to challenge to call to action.

callouts.p: A speech is composed for voice, breath and audience reaction, not only for silent reading.
If a phrase gains force when spoken, name the oral convention it uses.
A commemorative or formal address can be solemn, ceremonial and highly structured.

core.p: **Journals** and **reference book extracts** both organise knowledge, but they do different jobs. A journal is signalled by records over time or periodical conventions; a reference extract is built for looking up, checking and classifying information.
bullets: Journal cues include dates, entries, regular publication, reflection or subject headings; read the extract to decide which kind it is.
Reference cues include title, headings, subheadings, glossary, index, cross-reference, table or diagram.
Reference extracts often use impersonal register, technical terms and present tense for lasting truth.
Definitions, classification and examples are common reference moves.
Selection is still a choice: what is included, ordered or omitted shapes the reader.
Do not confuse a journal with journalism; one records or specialises, the other addresses a public news audience.

callouts.p: A passage from a book meant for looking up information; it uses headings, definitions, classification, glossaries, tables or diagrams and an impersonal register.
Say dated entry, glossary, heading or definition, then explain what that cue lets the reader do.
A reference extract aims for accuracy, but choice of definition, example and emphasis still presents a perspective.

core.h: Literary non-fiction: truth told with craft
core.p: **Literary non-fiction** uses true material but shapes it like literature. The writer is not inventing events; the writer is selecting, ordering, voicing and colouring real experience so that it means something.
bullets: The spec names autobiography, letters and travel writing as examples.
Voice and selection matter: the same day can be a memory, a message or a journey.
Imagery, pace, contrast, chronology and reflection are craft choices, not fiction tricks.
Truth claims do not force neutral language; feeling can be precise.
Autobiography looks back; letters respond to an occasion; travel writing moves through place.
Always tie a literary device to the real material it is shaping.

callouts.p: True material shaped by literary methods such as voice, image, structure, selection and reflection; it is not invented fiction.
The examiner rewards the link between true content and crafted presentation.
Do not call imagery or anecdote evidence that the text is fictional.

core.h: Autobiography, letters and travel writing compared
core.p: These three forms are all literary non-fiction, but the **reader relationship** changes. Autobiography addresses a public reader from memory; a letter addresses a named recipient from an occasion; travel writing addresses a reader through movement and place.
bullets: Autobiography: retrospective first person, selected episodes, reflection, shaped life narrative.
Letter: salutation, sign-off, date or place, shared knowledge, tone set by relationship.
Travel writing: journey structure, observation, sensory detail, fact and personal response.
The same event can be autobiographical memory, letter news or travel description.
Letters can be private, open or published; use the text cues, not assumptions.
Autobiography is not a diary: it is re-shaped after the fact for a reader.

callouts.p: Ask who is addressed, when, and why that changes the language.
Calling all of them personal misses the different jobs they do.

core.h: Prove the text type in three moves
core.p: Use **cue, convention, consequence**: name the visible feature, say what that feature normally does, then explain why it matters for meaning. This turns genre-spotting into evidence.
bullets: Cue: headline, salutation, glossary, dated entry, rating, diagram, sign-off.
Convention: what that cue expects in this text type, such as scan, judge, listen or look up.
Consequence: how the convention focuses attention, builds trust, creates rhythm or shapes response.
Quote short and exact; do not paraphrase the cue into vagueness.
If forms blend, say which dominates and which convention is borrowed.
Use the spec words: journalism, article, review, speech, journal, reference book extract, autobiography, letter, travel writing.

callouts.p: Cue is the visible sign; convention is its expected job; consequence is the effect on meaning.
One cue plus one convention plus one consequence is stronger than three labels.
A rhetorical question is not a point until you say it suits a speech to an audience.

core.p: Top answers treat text type as an argument about expectations, not as a sticker. They notice when a writer borrows another form’s conventions and they say whether that borrowing makes the text more public, more intimate, more authoritative or more vivid.
bullets: Watch mixed forms: a review using travel imagery, a speech printed as an article, a reference extract using examples.
Check century cues, but do not over-claim attitudes from one word.
There are no set texts for this point; the extract supplies everything needed.
This point has no separate Higher-tier or triple-only list; do not import science-style tiers.
Keep terminology exact: article, review, speech, journal, reference book extract, autobiography, letter, travel writing.
Judge a feature by the form’s job, not by whether you like it.
Practise one-sentence form naming: this is a review because it names criteria, judges and recommends.

callouts.p: Success is measured against what that text type is trying to do for its reader or listener.
Write form, audience, mode, cue before you write paragraphs.
This point is the genre range; do not turn it into a full method for every reading question.

analogy.t: Text types are like shop fronts
analogy.p: A bakery, a chemist and a library can all contain words, but the sign, layout and expected behaviour tell you how to use them: a headline is the shop window, a glossary is the labelled shelf, a salutation is being greeted by name. The analogy breaks because texts can deliberately mix shop fronts, and readers bring history, relationship and context that a fixed shop sign cannot control.

terms.d: Writing that presents real people, events, places or ideas; it can still be selective, shaped and opinionated.
A recognised form such as article, review, speech, journal, reference book extract, autobiography, letter or travel writing; its conventions create reader expectations.
A feature an audience expects from a text type, such as a headline, salutation, glossary, dated entry or rating.
The level and style of language chosen for audience, purpose and form; it can be formal, informal, technical or personal.
Public, timely non-fiction for readers; in this spec it includes articles and reviews.
A text that judges a book, film, performance, product or place against stated or implied criteria and guides the reader.
A text planned for delivery to an audience on an occasion; print may preserve oral cues such as address, pause and repetition.
A record form signalled by cues such as dates, entries, regular publication, reflection or subject headings; read the extract to decide which kind of journal it is.
A passage from a book meant for looking up information; it uses headings, definitions, classification, glossaries, tables or diagrams and an impersonal register.
True material shaped by literary methods such as voice, image, structure, selection and reflection; it is not invented fiction.
A first-person retrospective account of the writer's own life, selected and organised for a reader.
Writing addressed to a specific recipient; salutation, sign-off, shared knowledge and relationship shape tone and structure.
Non-fiction that records journeys and places, blending observation, description, fact and personal response.
The particular stance a writer takes, shown by what is selected, emphasised, omitted or praised.

mistakes.w: This is journalism because it has facts.
mistakes.r: Name the specific text type and prove it with a convention; reference extracts and travel writing can also contain facts.

mistakes.w: A review is just the writer's opinion.
mistakes.r: A review makes judgements against criteria and guides the reader; support the judgement with evidence from the extract.

mistakes.w: Speeches are informal because they are spoken.
mistakes.r: Speeches can be formal or ceremonial; use occasion, address and oral conventions to decide.

mistakes.w: Autobiography and journal mean the same thing.
mistakes.r: Autobiography is a retrospective shaped life narrative; a journal is signalled by dated entries, regular publication or reflective record cues.

mistakes.w: Reference book extracts have no viewpoint.
mistakes.r: They aim for accuracy, but definition, selection, example and emphasis still present a perspective.

mistakes.w: Travel writing is only description.
mistakes.r: It blends observation, movement, fact and personal response; explain the mix, not just the imagery.

mistakes.w: Letters must be private and unpublished.
mistakes.r: Letters can be private, open or published; identify them by salutation, sign-off, relationship and occasion.

mistakes.w: Literary non-fiction is fiction because it uses imagery.
mistakes.r: Literary non-fiction uses literary craft on true material; the method does not make the content invented.

exam.q: Name one text type from the spec list that is planned to be delivered aloud, and give one oral cue you might see.
model: Speech
Cue such as direct address, rhetorical question, repetition or salutation
exam.tip: Say the form, then one cue; do not just write persuasive.

exam.q: Give two conventions you would expect in a review.
model: Names the subject being reviewed
States a judgement or criterion
Uses evidence, rating or recommendation
exam.tip: Two distinct conventions beat two examples of the same opinion.

exam.q: An extract has a headline, byline, short paragraphs and a quoted expert. Identify the text type and explain why two cues fit it.
model: Journalism article
Headline signals public, timely reading
Byline signals a named writer for a readership
Quoted expert supports information or argument
exam.tip: Link each cue to the reader's job, do not only list features.

exam.q: How does a speech differ from an article in the way it addresses the audience? Refer to two features.
model: Speech addresses listeners through direct address and oral rhythm
Article addresses readers through headline, layout and paragraphs
Speech may use repetition, rhetorical question or pause
Article may use standfirst, byline or presentational features
exam.tip: Use listener for speech and reader for article; mode is the difference.

exam.q: A student says travel writing is just description. Correct this using the term literary non-fiction.
model: Travel writing is literary non-fiction
It records real places or journeys
It blends observation, fact, movement and personal response
Description is shaped by selection, voice and structure
exam.tip: Remove the word just by naming the blend.

exam.q: Compare how an autobiography and a letter can present the same real event. Name one convention of each and explain how the reader relationship changes the presentation.
model: Autobiography uses retrospective first person and shaped chronology for a public reader
Letter uses salutation, sign-off and shared knowledge for a named recipient
Same event is selected differently because the reader relationship differs
Register changes: memory and reflection versus immediacy and address
Use exact terms convention, register and perspective
Judgement is evidence-led, not based on topic alone
exam.tip: Keep both halves balanced and anchor each form in one visible convention.

worked.q: An extract opens with a headline, has a byline, uses short paragraphs and ends with a quoted specialist. Name the strongest text type and prove it.
steps: Find cues: headline, byline, short paragraphs, quotation.
Match cues to convention: public, timely reading for a readership.
Name the exact form: journalism article.
Write consequence: the cues help the reader scan, trust and continue.
worked.ans: This is most likely a journalism article because the headline and byline signal public reporting, while the short paragraphs and quoted specialist help a reader scan and check the information.

worked.q: A film piece gives three stars, calls the plot sluggish, praises the acting and says see it for the performances. Explain two review conventions.
steps: Identify criteria: plot and acting.
Identify judgement: sluggish plot, praised acting.
Identify guidance: three stars and see it for the performances.
Link convention to reader job: the reader is being guided, not merely told a plot.
worked.ans: The piece is a review because it judges against criteria such as plot and acting, then guides the reader with a rating and a recommendation; the praise of acting shows the judgement is supported, not just liked.
